pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 190: Practicing: speaking. Results: getting better.*

I cannot look people in the eye. I can, however, look a rose in the eye. It is a distinction I am choosing to make.

I stood in the Spring Room, facing the pear tree. My hands were shaking, so I held my tape measure tight to stop them from flapping. "This garden is not a car park," I said to the leaves. My voice came out thin, like a wire pulled too tight. I stopped. I took a breath that tasted of cold air and dirt. I tried again. "It has history. It has life. It is worth saving."

The roses did not laugh. The pear tree did not drop a fruit on my head. Nothing happened. The silence sat on my shoulders, heavy as a wet wool blanket. I straightened my glasses. I was not done. I said it again, louder this time, pushing the words out of my chest and into the air. "We need this place to breathe."

On the third try, I felt the hair on my arms stand up. The air in the room changed. It got thick and sweet. I looked at the rose bush nearest to me. A bud, tight and green, was opening. Not all at once, but slowly, petal by petal, unfolding in the cold light.

I want to say I felt proud. I felt mostly relieved that the plant had not judged me.
pages.image: Sana, a thin 11-year-old girl with brown skin, round glasses, and a low black bun with a green pencil, stands in a walled garden facing a large rose bush; her hands are clasped tight around a tape measure, and a single red rose is slowly opening in the cold morning light.

pages.text:
Theo sat on the humming bench, skates tucked under one arm, having listened for twenty minutes without turning his head. His beanie was pulled low, and his hoodie sleeves were pushed up to his elbows, revealing pale forearms that looked like they had never seen the sun.

"You kept saying sorry," he said, staring at the concrete. "Why do you keep apologizing for existing?"

"I was being polite," I replied, adjusting my glasses.

"You were wasting time." He pointed a finger at my denim jacket. "Drop the 'just.' Stop looking at your shoes. You are talking to the ground, and the ground cannot save you."

"That is very rude," I said, "for someone who has never spoken in class either."

He shrugged, a small, sharp movement. "Exactly why. I know how it feels to freeze. So stop freezing and start talking."

We practiced until the streetlights flickered on outside the wall, turning the sky the color of old dishwater. I got better. Not great, but better. My voice stopped shaking, and my words stopped stumbling over each other like Yusuf’s toys in the hallway. Theo finally looked at me, his eyes bright and unreadable.

"Okay," he said. "That was less terrible."

It was the highest compliment I had ever received, and I accepted it with a nod.
pages.image: Theo, a 12-year-old boy in a beanie and hoodie with pushed-up sleeves, sits on a stone bench in a garden at twilight, pointing a finger at Sana, who stands holding a tape measure; the streetlights outside the wall are just beginning to glow orange.

pages.text:
Yusuf is a leaky faucet. You cannot plug him. You cannot cover him with a cloth. He simply tells the truth, loudly, and everywhere.

"Did you hear about the tortoise?" he announced to Mrs. Ilves, who was hanging her washing. "He is three hundred years old. He eats lettuce. He is very wise. He says 'Mm. Not yet.' It is very funny."

By Friday, the rumor had traveled from Block C to Block A. It moved through the estate on the old-fashioned network of windowsills and open doors. People stopped me in the lift. They stared at my patched pockets, which held seed packets. They looked at my green pencil. They asked, with a suspicion that was almost funny, if I was trying to sell them something.

I did not sell them anything. I only pointed toward the loading bay.

That evening, a crowd gathered at the gap in the fence. There was Mrs. Ilves, knitting a scarf. There was Nadia Okafor, holding her mother’s hand. There were three men from Block A who wore coats that had seen better decades. They stood in a line, arms crossed, eyes narrowed.

"A tortoise," the tallest one said. "In this mess?"

"Impossible," said Mrs. Ilves.

"Ridiculous," said Nadia’s mother.

I opened the gate. The hinges creaked, a sound like a knee bending. The crowd stepped forward. They stopped. They looked at the mossy shell. They looked at the green leaves. And then, one by one, they went quiet.
pages.image: A group of neighbors, including an older woman knitting and men in coats, stand at the open iron gate of a walled garden, looking down with wide eyes at a small, mossy tortoise sitting on a stone path in the greenery.

pages.text:
The garden did not explain itself; it simply reacted.

As the neighbors stepped onto the paving, the roses in the Spring Room began to bloom. It was not a sudden explosion. It was a slow, deepening of color, green turning to pink, then pink turning to red. The air smelled of wet earth and lemon zest. The bench, which usually hummed only when I told the truth, began to vibrate. It was a low, steady note, like a single, gentle hand playing a church organ.

Mr. Osei stood by the door, his ring of keys jingling softly as he shifted his weight. He did not speak, and he did not need to. The garden was speaking for him.

The three men from Block A looked at each other. Their suspicion drained out of their faces, replaced by something softer, sadder.

"I was here," one of them said, his voice rough. "Before the fence went up. I played here. I had a bike."

"Me too," said the second man. "We caught beetles."

"I remember the pear tree," said the third. "It was smaller. Or I was smaller."

They did not laugh, and they did not make jokes. They stood in the circle of green, surrounded by the blooming roses, and for a moment, the concrete estate behind them seemed very far away.
pages.image: Three older men stand in a walled garden, looking down at a small tortoise; behind them, a row of red roses is in full bloom, and a stone bench sits in the foreground, emitting a faint, warm glow.

pages.text:
They started bringing things. Not gifts, exactly, but words.

A woman from the ninth floor walked to the edge of the Summer Room, looking at her hands, then at the dirt. "I am afraid I will fail my exam," she said, and her voice was small. A tomato vine, heavy with red fruit, turned toward her. The fruit ripened, turning from green to bright red in the space of a breath.

A boy, maybe ten, stood by the pear tree. "I do not like the new school," he said. The leaves rustled, a sound like applause.

An old man from Block A said nothing for a long time. He stood by the iron gate, his hands in his pockets, while the wind blew his grey hair across his forehead. He did not move, and the garden waited, refusing to rush him.

Finally, he looked at the tortoise. "I miss her," he whispered. "My wife. She used to come here."

The bench hummed with a deep, resonant warmth. Mr. Osei stood by the gate, his hand on the iron, his eyes shut and his shoulders shaking just slightly. He did not step inside. He did not have to. The garden had heard him.
pages.image: An elderly man with grey hair stands at an iron garden gate, his hand resting on the bar; he has his eyes closed, and beside him, a small tortoise sits on the stone path, with a row of ripe red tomatoes hanging on a vine nearby.
